speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When this matter was presented to the House at the first reading I made a statement as to its general purpose and some discusion took place then which I am sure enabled the House to understand the aim of the Bill. I did not, however, at that time, give any information as to what might be the expense involved in the adoption of this measure and I think the committee would desire to be informed on that point The Bill provides that the system may be administered from time to time by any minister to whom the business may be assigned, but for the present it shall be assigned to the Minister of Tr^le and Commerce. As hon. gentlemen know, my hon. colleague who holds that office has given great attention to the subject and his name has been particularly identified with its promotion. I have asked him to advise me as to what expenditure would be incurred and he thinks that the total expenses, in the early days at any rate, would not exceed $50,000 a year, and would only reach that amount if the system were availed of to a considerable extent. It would be necessary to appoint an officer who perhaps might be called the superintendent and some three or four others who, under his directions, might be required to travel over the country and make known the object and machinery of the Act. I think we would also need a government actuary. My intention is that that office shall be attached to the Department of Finance, for this reason, that our actuarial work is growing and we have a considerable amount of that work, which has hitherto been performed by the super-tendent of insurance, and which with the additional work involved in this scheme, will warrant the appointment of a special actuary. Further, the superintendent of insurance and his staff are practically not paid by the country at all, but by the insur-

10S50
ance companies. The expenses of the office are a charge on these companies, and it would be hardly fair to load them with expenses not connected with their business but purely with government business. Although that matter is not finally determined, I think we shall require a government actuary who will advise the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the administration of this Act and other Departments on like matters such as the provident fund of the Intercolonial, the pension of militia and Mounted Police and our own superannuation fund. I assume that some proportion of that work will be assigned to the officer I have described, and there will be in the Department of Trade and Commerce the superintendent and some three or four men appointed to travel over the Dominion and explain the system. The Bill has aroused very considerable attention. There was a tendency at first to associate it with old age pensions, but it does not profess to be an old age pension Bill. It is not a Bill in which the country provides old age pensions but a system whereby parties may purchase annuities for their old age. I do not think I can add anything by way of information. We shall have to take a vote in the supplementaries for whatever sum may be deemed necessary in the administration of the Act.
Have there been any protests from mutual insurance companies and others against the Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking from memory, I do not think there have been. This does mu come seriously into conflict with the insurance companies for this reason, that although they have the power to issue annuities they have not gone into that line to any extent. In proportion to the amount and number of other policies issued, the number of annuity policies is quite small.
Is it the intention to have an agent representing the government in each county ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is not contemplated to appoint more than four or five officers at the outside, some of whom would visit the various parts of Canada and endeavour to interest the public in the Act. There would be no special officers appointed at the beginning outside the number I have indicated, but we hope to be able to utilize the existing public officers. For example postmasters, collectors of customs or any important public officers might be interested and be the instruments of making the Act known and some small commission would be allowed them on any business done. It is not intended to appoint any considerable number of officers in the beginning.
Is this to be self-sustaining ? Will the charges come out of the funds of the Dominion or will the fund that accumulates pav for the salaries ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The expenses of management will be a charge on the government generally and in that respect it will not be self-sustaining.
In that respect alone ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we allow a rate of interest as high as four per cent, that might be deemed to be some concession to the annuitant because money might be really worth a little less. Unless in the rate of interest being more than the ordinary, that is the only concession the annuitant gets.

I think I said, when the Bill was up before, that I thought, taking economy and efficiency into account, it is the Postmaster General who ought to administer this Act. He has his offices spread over the whole country. He has in every district some one who represents him. He has offices in which this scheme could be put in operation and be prominently adverr lised so that every man who wanted to purchase an annuity-whether a resident in a far rural district or in a city-would have an equal opportunity to get whatever benefits there are to be derived from it, if there are any. The substitution of four or five men travelling throughout the country in order to make this scheme known seems its own condemnation. If it is a scheme for the general benefit of the country, then it ought to he brought to the minds of the country generally. But how much ground can four travellers cover and in what way will they spread the knowledge of this scheme ? If it is going to be worked out at all and you are going to take that method you will require a good many more than three or four travellers. It would be far better to utilize the post offices. Make out a clear and brief description of your scheme, let the public know its conditions and rates, and that application forms are to be had at the post offices. There you have a complete machinery at a minimum cost. Suppose you add a slight commission to the postmaster on every annuity sold by him, you will have to pay a commission anyway. By this means you would get at-everybody. The post office is always in a central place, the postmaster is seen by every one, and lie has every opportunity to promote this pian.
Now, I quite know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been, as it were, the father of the scheme, and I suppose it is natural that he should want to manage it. But he could use the post office machinery. and then, when he gets tired of fathering the scheme, he can hand it over to the Postmaster General and it would be then in a condition of permanency. But it will cost up to. probably, 850.000' for these other officers and general expenses, whereas. the other way the cost would be only a bagatelle. All that would be required

would be an actuary, if you have not. already an actuary whose advice you could take. I suppose that the business of an actuary in the matter would not go further than the formulating of the scheme, preparing tables of rates and so on. I think it a question worthy of consideration whether you are going to duplicate machinery and be efficient or use the machinery of the Post Office Department and be efficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With most of what the hon. member (Mr. Foster) says I can quite agree, especially with regard to utilizing the machinery of the Post Office Department. But I think that what he suggests will be done in any case. There will be a distribution of literature and forms relating to the plan, and a very considerable proportion of the expense will be this distribution of literature to inform the public. The only difference between what he has suggested, and what I have mentioned is that he questions whether there will be need for these three or four additional officers. But some means must be taken to bring the advantages of the scheme directly to the attention of the public. The insurance companies have the same experience. We all know that life insurance is a most excellent thing, and yet nine out of ten men never take insurance until somebody comes and presses them to do so. That is the experience of mankind. The mere fact that a thing is good in itself does not mean that it will be taken up by the public. Even the best things of life have to be recommended. Though I believe this to be an excellent scheme, founded on sound principles and calculated to do much good, I do not anticipate that the public will rush after it unless somebody takes pains to explain its merits and advantages. But the machinery of the Post Office Department will certainly be used, and, to a certain extent, if possible, the machinery of other departments. The fact that the direction is first assigned to the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not inconsistent with its being assigned to some other department in the future if, at a larger stage, it should be deemed advisable. I think the hon. gentleman is right that the Post Office Department, in that case, will be the best. We certainly will employ all the machinery of the post office to do all the hon. gentleman suggests in the way of making the plan known. But, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce appoints three or four men to make known the merits of the scheme and enlist public sympathy, he will be doing in a small way what all the insurance companies do.
Does the Minister of Finance think it wise to enter into an active propaganda in competition with insurance companies ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

And with the fraternal orders ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) said, and seemed to think when he made the statement, he made the whole case for interference with these two kinds of organizations, that the fraternal orders and insurance companies do not sell many annuities. But I do not think he did make the case. In proportion as you persuade any man to buy an annuity you probably cut out a prospective member of a fraternal organization, benefit society or insurance company. It will certainly tend in that way. Now, while it is fair that the government should make provision whereby the citizens of the country can purchase annuities, is it quite right and proper for the government to enter into an active canvassing propaganda in favour of that plan as against the insurance company and the benefit and fraternal societies ? I scarcely think it is. I think the government does its duty when it places the'information before the people through some such means as the machinery of the post office, and allows every man to use his own judgment with reference to it. But I think the government goes too far when it enters into an active propaganda. If there is any argument for the five travellers, there is an argument for five hundred in exactly the same way, and so you go on expanding expense that I do not think we ought to incur. I believe that it will affect very materially the fraternal organizations and insurance companies in that, if yon persuade five thousand people to take annuities, you probably have persuaded a very large proportion who would otherwise become members of the fraternal organizations or seek insurance benefits, to refrain from doing so, or to drop their relations to these companies. I think you affect these organizations more, perhaps, than the minister thinks-certainly more than, from the expressions he has made use of as to the efforts to be put forth in selling annuities, the House would be led to believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) I think, on looking at the matter more closely will find that his criticism is hardly supported by the facts. I may remind the hon. gentleman of a fact which must have been called to his attention that, though the insurance companies have always been authorized to carry on annuity business, the annuities carried by these companies in Canada number only 1,321, and the average is only $270. That is practically the insurance companies do not do an annuity business. They do not make an effort to press that business. Therefore, we are not competing with them. As to the benefit and fraternal societies, he will find, if he looks into the matter, that they do not do annuity business-they are forbidden by the Act to do flint business, except in one case which may be considered a partial exception. The

Foresters are allowed to do what is not exactly an annuity business, but is somewhat different from the ordinary plan; they are allowed to distribute the payment of the capital sum over a numoei1 of years. For example, if a policy of $10,000*matured, instead of being obliged to pay the $10,000 at once, it can be arranged that it shall be paid at the rate of $1,000 a year for ten years. But the hon. gentleman will see at once that that is not a system of life annuities. The policy of our insurance legislation has always been that these fraternal organizations should not be encouraged to do annuity business. They fill their place and carry on their special work. They offer fraternal and social advantages and benefits for wThich many men are glad to join them. If there were insurance companies or fraternal societies carrying on this business widely and efficiently, there would be less reason for this measure. In that case, all we would have to offer would be the absolute security which characterizes a government institution, and that alone probably would not be enough to make this measure necessary. But, the fact being that the insurance companies do not do this business and that the fraternal societies do not and must not do it, there is an immense field to be occupied. My only fear in the matter is that, good as the system is it will not be readily taken up by the multitude because their attention has not been drawn to it. Therefore, I think the action of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in employing three or four men to travel about the country and make known the advantage of the system is meritorious. If it prove that, even then, it cannot be done, the only result will be that we shall have spent a little money in an effort to promote a good movement. An appropriation of $25,000 will be sufficient to cover this at the start and it is believed that the total for some years will not exceed $50,000, including salaries, commissions, printing, distribution of literature and everything else. I think the effort a good one and well worth making.

There are companies in Canada doing an annuity business to which the hon. minister (Mr. Fielding) has not referred. The Great West Company, which is a very strong and popular company, in Western Canada, offers an annuity policy on -which, for instance, on a policy of $3,000, $150 a year is paid for twenty years. I know that, as a matter of fact, the Great West does business along that line. As to the other companies, I am not so well informed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not a case of life annuity. It only means that the policy is paid in instalments extending over a number of years. The object of this Bill is to provide that a man can purchase au annuity based on his expectation of life.
That is not being done, as I have said, either by insurance companies or fraternal societies. We are not competing with those organizations. As I have said, my only doubt is whether we can succeed in getting the people interested. I come back to the same illustration as before : insurance is a good thing, but none of us take out insurance as a matter of fact until some gentlemanly agent comes and presses us to do so.

There was a company organized in Winnipeg about two years ago, called the Annuity Company of Canada to carry on this business. But they did not seem to meet with very flattering success. The people who took stock practically lost all the money they put into it, because the company was not able to get the business to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe they have gone out of business.

Because they could not get business to do. There seemed to be an apathy on the part of the public in regard to taking out those annuities. Now so far as the appointment of travelling agents is concerned, it would seem to me that if they are of any use at all, they must go and canvass for persons, and if you only appointed four or five, you could not possibly cover the whole Dominion, they must be confined to comparatively small localities. If it is a good thing to canvas for this business, you want to have a sufficient number to cover the whole country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not in the Bill, that is a matter of machinery.

I think that part of the machinery had better be left out, and you had better confine it to the postmasters, who would be in a position to canvass to a certain extent, or at least, let the people know that they can get these annuities. I think it is a good thing that there should be an opportunity for people to take out annuities, so that a man may, when his time of active work is ended, have some assured income from the result of his activity when he is able to earn money. But in regulating the machinery I think you ought to confine the canvassing to postmasters and to collectors of customs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The machinery is not regulated by the Bill. I have no doubt the minister will have his attention drawn to all the opinions expressed in the House, and will profit by them. I asked him to give an indication of what he had in his mind and he mentioned the appointment of these three or four officers, and that is why I mention them to the House.
On section 4,
What is meant by ' immediate ' as distinguished from ' deferred ' annuity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An immediate annuity is one the benefit of which comes to the party immediately ; a deferred annuity is one which would give him an annuity beginning at a date to be fixed.
What is the definition of the term ' domiciled in Canada ' for application under the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That means residence in Canada, one whose home and residence is in Canada. I think the word ' domiciled ' has a legal meaning.
On section 5, payments by purchaser.
Why do you put that amount at $10?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object is that he may make his payment at a stated time, or if he does not wish to be bound to stated times, then whenever he has $10 or more he can deposit it, and have the value placed to his credit.
But you would not give an annuity on the basis of $10?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The theory is that a party might put in $10, and the next month another $10, and he would put it in at irregular intervals, then he could get the annuity to the aggregate value of his contributions. Or you can pay it like an insurance premium at a stipulated time, and you get interest from the date of each payment. Under the first plan he need not make any periodical payment at all. If he prefers to put in a periodical payment he is credited with interest from the date of payment, practically the same as in the savings bank.
On section 6, annuity tables.
Mi-. FOWLER. Are these tables prepared ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that will be a work for the government.
What interest do you pay ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have not contemplated paying more than 4 per cent, possibly a little less, but certainly not more. The rate may be changed from time to time according to monetary conditions.
On section 7, limitations as to persons and amounts.
Why limit it to $600?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not designed to furnish annuities for wealthy people. It is for, I do not say poor people, but those who may be called people of moderate means, to whom a $600 annuity is a considerable sum. We think it is not desirable, inasmuch as the government have to contribute in some way to it, to make the annuity large enough to attract men who can provide for themselves otherwise.
I thought the scheme of the Act was that the fund would be self supporting ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would depend upon the rate of interest. For example, if we allowed 4 per cent when the value of money is only 34 per cent, then to the extent of that 4 per cent we are giving a concession, and in that case the expenses of administration would be a charge upon the public treasury, and to that extent it would not be self-supporting.
I understood from the explanation of the minister at a former stage of the Bill that the expenses of administration would not be a charge upon the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be a charge on the public, but not on the funds.
Apart from that, I understand that the scheme was that the fund would be self-supporting, but the minister thinks that may be departed from to the extent of a small amount of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we say that 4 per cent is the proper value of money and if we allow 4 per cent, then it is self-supporting. If we allow 4 per cent when money was only worth 34 per cent, we are to that extent giving a little concession to the annuitant. But as that is in the interest of thrift, I do not think anybody will object.
Will these annuities be taxable by the municipalities ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we will have power to exempt them from taxation, that I fancy would be a provincial matter. But we do provide that they shall be exempt from seizure. But they would have to be subject, I presume, to the laws of the province with respect to the income tax.
If the fund is to be self-supporting, there is no advantage in this Bill beyond what any one would derive from putting his money in the government savings bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. This simply gives a person the security of the government. It does not profess to be any great concession to the annuitant any more than the savings bank itself is a concession. It gives him a safe investment.

That all depends upon the tables of mortality. IHe pays in a certain amount of money. Say that he pays in $2,000, he gets an annuity of $400 a year after a certain time, but on his death the principal sum which he has paid in goes into the treasury. Is that not it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is it. But that, of course, as in the insurance business, is dependent upon the tables of mortality. The calculation is based upon the ordinary

expectation of life. If the ordinary expectation of life is realized it just reverses itself. It may be that it will turn one way or the other, but the tables of mortality will be framed on the basis of the fund simply being of self-sustaining subject to the qualification about the rate of interest.
The government pays interest at the rate of 4 per cent on the principal until the death of the annuitant; four l>er cent is not a high rate of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He does not get merely 4 per cent ; he gets an annuity based upon a 4 per cent calculation.

As I understand the Finance Minister, this result will follow that if a man at the age of 30 agreed that he would make periodical payments and died at the age of 54 he would receive back his money with interest compounded at 3 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
But if he should live until he was 50 he would simply get his annuity for one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Euless he stipulated a different condition when he took out his policy.
But that could occur under this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He might have an annuity which would run for a given number of years. But speaking generally, what my hon. friend says will be correct. Assuming that a man takes an annuity dependent upon his life, that is th? risk that is to be taken. It may be so in some cases, but on the average there will be no gain to the fund. There may be a particular case in which a man would pay a particular sum and get a very small annuity. That would depend what the variation, one way or the other, from the average mortality would be.
It Is just a question of the expectation of life.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Why do you make a limit of 55 years? Do you think that he has reached the limit of his earning power?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, it is not desirable to provide annuities for person in middle life ; 55 years may be taken as perhaps as good a figure ns you can mention for the termination of the earning period of a man's life.
Section 2, subsection 3-maximum age,
Why is that provision necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is copied from the British government scheme. The intention is to prevent speculation in annuities for persons of great age.
On section 8-minister may refuse to contract where he is of opinion that there are sufficient grounds,
How do you regulate that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I confess I do not know what that means except that if under any exceptional circumstances the minister should think that the person should not receive an annuity he is not obliged to give it to him. I do not think it amounts to very much, because I cannot think of any circumstances under which the minister would be justified in refusing.

It seems to me rather a dangerous provision. We ought to know the circumstances under which the minister would refuse to enter into a contract. A party might have enemies and statements derogatory to his character might be made to the minister. It does not seem to me that the minister should have this discretion unless there are some grounds stated. It should be defined.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I confess there will be great difficulty in defining it, because I could not state any class of circumstances which would justify the refusal of an annuity. There might be a case in which the minister might have reason to believe that there was some fraudulent element in it or it might be a case of insanity or something like that. It seems to me that all it means is that you are not obliged to give an annuity to anybody if some exceptional circumstances shoull arise. I cannot conceive of any circumstancfs which would justify the minister in refusing an annuity.
As far as insanity is concerned that might be set out as a cause for refusal in the Bill. I think there is a possibility of hardship under it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An insurance company is not bound to issue a policy to a man if it does not want to, and this simply says that if any difficulty should arise you are not obliged' to give a man an annuity.
The lowest or any tender not necessarily accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That fairly illustrates it.
I think the clause should be worded in such a way as to provide some rule for the guidance of the minI ister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend suggest anything?
Mr, LANCASTER. No, because I do not see any need for this section myself. If there is a reason I think it ought to be, within reasonable limits defined, so as to have some rule for the guidance of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Every insurance company has the same condition.
An ordinary insurance company is in a different position. The public are undertaking to do this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that the same clause is in the British Act and I would suggest that the hon. gentleman accept it.
As far as 1 am personally concerned that is a good reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest that hon. gentlemen accept the clause and if any case should arise in which there seemed to be an abuse I am sure that parliament would quickly strike the clause out.
In clause 10 there does not seem to be any provision as to how the minister shall be notified of the judgment of the court, nor does it seem to provide for an appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I fancy that while there is an appeal pending the minister would not act until the judgment of the final court was obtained. The parties interested would take care the minister was notified.
The minister should have something to guide him as to what he would take as notice.
That could be provided for in the regulations under section 12.

It strikes me that the words in section 10 are not quite full enough. I think that after the word ' creditors ' there should be inserted the words ' and has that effect.' A man might do a thing with intent, but did not accomplish it, and if no one was defrauded the section should not apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it did not defraud any one we would not be asked to give any one the benefit of the section.
Mr. LANCASTER I am not quarrelling with the meaning of the section, but it would strike me that the language used might not give effect to our meaning. If there were simply an intent and the intent were established, without fraud being committed, I do not think the annuity should be interfered with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He would not be in a position to claim under this clause unless there was loss.
Every man at some stage of his life has creditors, and a man

may do a thing with intent to defraud his creditors at the time he did it, but he may cure it and something may happen which would prevent the creditors being defrauded. This section says that if you establish there was an intent to defraud the section should apply. What I submit is that the intent should result in actual fraud.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the court give judgment of fraud unless a fraud had actually occurred ?
No, but you say that if the court finds there was intent to defraud only the annuity should be interfered with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend and I have the same object, but I fear to accept this amendment to a Bill which has been considered carefully by the legal advisers of the government. I will take a note of my hon. friend's observations, and if it is found necessary then in another place which sometimes fixes things, it may be put right.
No doubt this language has been selected because it is practically the language of the English statute.

The language of the Ontario statute in regard to defaulting creditors is different. I do not say the language is wrong as it is, but we might make plain what we all mean. If a court found there was intent to defraud although there was no actual fraud, a thing which occurs often in mercantile life, the language of this section would then apply. By the exact language of the Act as it is to-day, all that would have to be established wouid be that at some time the man had an intent of committing a fraud, not carried out, and the result, even although there was no actual wrong from it, would be to interfere with the annuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will allow this to stand for third reading until we can have the opinion of the minister of Justice on the matter.

At the death of the annuitant previous to the age of 55 years the money is distributed among his heirs. If he passes away after receiving his annuity for a year or more, what would be done with the balance of the money to his credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would depend on the kind of annuity he bought. If it was a given term of years not dependent on his life, the annuity would have to be paid for the term of years, but in the case of a life annuity it would be paid only so long as he lived, then it would terminate. All that would enter into the question of the average mortality in fixing the tables.
Then if he had received one payment of the annuity his heirs would receive nothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not unless he had stipulated in his policy that it should be for a given time.

In respect to the point raised by the hon. member for Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) the statute in its present form would be very suitable to the province of Nova Scotia, with the laws of which I am more particularly acquainted, but I can see the possibility of dimculty with regard to the operation in other provinces where the terms of the old English statute, which are practically embodied here, may have been varied by legislation. With respect to clause 12, I think it should embody a provision for placing before parliament these regulations at an early date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think tnat is a very .desirable amendment and shall move it to clause 15.

I think no business should be done until parliament approves of the regulations.
iMr. FIELDING. People might die in the meantime.
Supposing after business has been done under these regulations they are laid before parliament and parliament does not pass them, it will make some difficulty with the contracts then in existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The regulations will very largely deal with technical work of an actuarial character on which my hon. friend and I will hardly care to pass an opinion. They would, of course, be In accordance with the provisions of this Act. I agree with the leader of the opposition that they should be submitted to parliament.
Then why have them come into force before bringing them before parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object in laying them before parliament is that parliament should be fully informed upon the whole matter. Many regulations are authorized by various Acts of parliament, to take effect as soon as they are made.

I fail to see why the regulations should not have been ready now. There are plenty of actuaries and this is not new ground.
On section 13,-returns of accounts, &c.
Will that include the expense of carrying on the Act that are to be paid out of the public moneys.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, yes, the returns will have to show how the thing stands.
On section 15,-returns to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move in accordance with the suggestion of the leader of the opposition to insert the words :
And copies of all regulations made during such fiscal year under the provisions of section 12 of this Act.
Would it not be better to say that this shall be done in the first 30 days of the session, otherwise they might be laid on the table on the last day of the session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no objection and would move to insert words to that effect.

I cannot quite understand how it can be fair to a man's family that after he has paid a number of years his annual payments and then dies before the age of fifty-five, this money is not returned to his family with interest at three per cent. If he has received two or three annuities which amount only to a part of the money he paid in, I cannot understand why his family should not get the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would strike at the vital condition of a life annuity. The same difficulty occurs under a superannuation system. An officer has paid in for twenty years and shortly before the period when, in the natural order of things, he would have to retire on his allowance, he dies. He has contributed large sums to Jhe superannuation fund and neither he nor his family gets a copper out of it. But all that enters into the computation of rates and risks taken. It is estimated that a man will live a given number of years. He lives less than the number but his neighbour lives longer. The tables are made on the average life. If there were not cases such as my hon. friend refers to. the rates would have to be higher. And the
And the amount of the annuity would be that much less.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he prefers to make a contract for an annuity to be paid during a given period, irrespective of death or life, he may do so. But if he makes purchase of a life annuity, he has to take his chances.

It is purely a gamble and the man takes his chances.
Bill reported.

After Recess.

Bill (No. 165) respecting the Court of Appeal of British Columbia.-Mr. Ayles-worth-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1-Disfranchising Act amended.
10S63

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COURT OF APPEAL OF BRITISH COLUMBIA.
speechtext:
This is to amend the section of the Disfranchising Act, which, as it stands, provides for appeals from the decision of any judge or court disfranchising the voter. Appeal is allowed to courts of the several provinces. I am proposing that this jurisdiction should be conferred upon the Court of Appeal for the province of British Columbia.
On section 2-amending section 102 of the Winding-up Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COURT OF APPEAL OF BRITISH COLUMBIA.
speechtext:
That section of the Winding-up Act has been amended during the present session so far as Manitoba is concerned. By that amendment, jurisdiction under that section of the Winding-up Act was conferred on the Court of Appeal for Manitoba, and, in view of that legislation, the clause should now read a little differently. I have redrawn it in this form, which I propose to substitute:
Section 102 of the Winding-up Aot, chapter 114 of the Revised Statutes. 1906, as said section is amended by an Aot passed in this present session of parliament, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
102. Such appeal shall lie-
(a)	In Ontario to the Court of Appeal for
Ontario;	.
(b)	In Quebec to the Court of King's Bench;
(c)	In Manitoba to the Court of Appeal;
(d)	In British Columbia to the Court of Appeal of the province; and
(e)	In any of the other provinces, and in the Yukon Territory, to a superior court en banc.

maintopic: COURT OF APPEAL OF BRITISH COLUMBIA.

The title is 4 An Act to amend the Winding-up Act.'
On section 4-amending paragraph (7) of section 2 of the Criminal Code.

House in Committee of Supply.
Public buildings in British Columbia-public building at Cranbrook, $7,000.

['We will take up the Bill to amend the Bank Act, the resolution respecting the lead bounty in British Columbia, the Bill to amend the Manitoba Grain Act and then Supply, my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works continuing his estimates.\nMotion agreed to and House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Friday.', 'Fbiday, June 19, 1908.']

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: This amount is for the purchase of a site and the erection of a building. There was an appropriation last year of $7,000, which has not been used. The purchase of the site has not been completed, although an agreement has been come to for the price of $9,000. Three lots have been selected after great care, having a frontage of 80 feet on Baker street by 120 upon Norman street. There was a good deal of negotiation before the department agreed to pay the price that was asked.
Were there any commissions paid?

No, the purchase was made directly by the department. The contract for the building has not yet been let, but it is supposed the cost will run from $25,000 to $30,000. Cranbrook is a rapidly growing town, with a population of about 3,500 now. The sum of $30,000 will not include the land. The plans will be prepared by the department. The building will be used for post office and customs purposes. We have been paying for post office accommodation $475, and for customs purposes $180. Cranbrook is in Kootenay.
Cumberland public building, $9,000.

This is a revote to make provision for the erection of a public building in the town of Cumberland. In this case the site has been paid for, and the contract entered into. The site costs $700, and is 44 x 44. Cumberland is in Comox-Atlin, with a population estimated at 3.500. The total cost of the building is estimated at $37,766, including everything.
There is an extraordinary difference between the cost of this site and the other. I am surprised at the price of land in Cranbrook.

I was too, and at first I refused to purchase. We had our clerk of works come from Vancouver to examine it, Mr. Henderson, who is a very reliable man, in whom the department has great confidence. I hesitated so much about purchasing that land that I sent for Mr Henderson from Vancouver to go and examine the site, aud the best he could do was to pay $9,000 for these three lots.

I think the minister would have acted wisely if he had delayed a few years and allowed these people to furnish the site themselves. I think it is an outrage to pay $9,000 for a site of the I size the minister has indicated, even in the

growing town of Cranbrook. No minister should have acquiesced in that transaction.

My hon. friend must see that if we are going to erect a public building in a town, we are necessarily obliged to pay what land is fairly worth, having regard to what other lots similarly situated are changing hands for. In the west the population is growing rapidly, and the value of property in the east is not a sure guide as to the value of property in the west, because the people are all looking forward to the future. The town is growing rapidly, and will soon have a large population.
When the lumber is cut out, what will become of Cranbrook? I happened to be there a few years ago, and all 1 could see was a lumber mill.

I understand that it is the distributing point for people engaged in the mining business, that it is the centre of a tine fruit growing district, a lumber manufacturing centre, and I am told that there are large areas of timber land which are tributary to it.
I assume that when the timber is cut the mills will move back.
Cranbrook is a good town.
From whom was the site purchased ?
Messrs. King & Beattie.
What business are they iu ?
Mr. King Is a doctor ; I do not know what business Mr. Beattie is in.
Mr. Beattie used to be a lumberman there.
What is the annual cost of the accommodation at that point ?
Post office $475, and customs $180.
What is the cost of the present accommodation at Cumberland ?
'What other purpose will this building serve ?
It is intended for customs purposes as well.
Is there a customs port there, and if so what rent is paid for the office 1

Cumberland is an out-port of Nanaimo at present but it is expected that a customs office will be established.
Apparently there is no rental paid for the outport.
We are going to spend upwards of $40,000 at a point where the post office is now kept up at an annual expenditure of $125.
Cumberland is the centre of one of the most important mining districts of British Columbia.
What is the population?
About 3,000.

I would like to remind the minister that I asked him a question with reference to the Dauphin public building at a recent sitting of the House and he promised to bring down a report on the valuation of the property purchased for a site as well as a report upon former transfers.

I do not think my hon. friend received a promise that I would bring down a report on former transfers because I would not be likely to have that in the department. That could only be obtained by an examination of the record office at Dauphin. My deputy tells me that he lias a report upon the transfer to the government and I will be very glad to produce it this evening.
I see that the postal revenue at Cumberland is $1,465.
That is for nine months. But, just to give an idea of the importance of the town, the money orders issued during the nine months were $58,566.29 and the money orders paid $7,726.
Do you not consider the postal revenue more of a criterion of the size and importance of a town than the volume of money orders ?

No, I would not necessarily.
Femie public building, $30,000.
This vote is to make provision for the erection of a public building in Femie. The site was purchased in 1905 at cost of $5,000. The work is under contract and is nearly completed.
cost ?

site ?
What will be the total It is estimated at $66,-Is that inclusive of the

That includes site, heating. electric wiring, fittings, furniture, lock boxes, &c.
Ladysmith public building, $10,000.

This is required for the erection of a public building at Ladysmith.

There was paid for the site $1,500. It is under contract also.
Let us have the particulars.
This is in the electoral division of Nanaimo, Vancouved island.
That is about 15 miles from Nanaimo and it is a large coal mining centre.
What is the population ?
About 4,500. It is an incorporated city and they have nothing but a small building.

The value of land in Nanaimo seems to be very much less than in Kootenay. It is a surprising difference. I would have thought that land would have been of as much value in Ladysmith as in the other important place called Cranbrook, where the astonishing sum of $9,000 was paid for a lot 120x80. It must be a surprise to members of this House how much money can be stowed away in a small piece of land in British Columbia.
I wonder that the hou. gentleman is not surprised that in Ladysmith we got it so cheaply.

No, that may be nearer the value. What I am surprised at is that the Minister of Public Works should have been induced to put away $9,000 in a small site in Cranbrook. It is an outrage and a waste of public money.

I think our friends in Ladysmith must not have become acquainted with the liberality of this government when they sold that lot for $1,500. The minister is to be complimented upon the bargain he made at Ladysmith, while in the other place he paid four or five times the value.
I try to get the business of the government done, as far as my influence goes, just the same as I do my own business.
Is it a corner lot ?

Yes, it is a very important iot and they bought it from a gentleman who produced his vouchers showing that he paid $1,500 for the lot. He was leaving and wanted to sell so he sold it to the government for what he paid for it to a dollar.
Quesnel public building, $2,000.

I move to strike out this item for the reason that there is a telegraph building which was erected recently by the telegraph department. The building has been erected by contract under the supervision of the general superintendent of government telegraph service at a cost of $2,000. It has been paid for and comes out of the telegraph vote.
Mr. PUGSLEY

It is interesting to see how the government is spending the money of the people in that country. They have been paying $20 a year for post office accommodation at Quesnel, and the gross revenue is only $326. It does not matter much which department is spending $2,000, it is simply throwing away money.
This building, which was erected for $2,000, is to be used as a post office and telegraph office and also as a living room for the telegraph agent.
I quite admit that all that may be true but why should the country be spending $2,000 for a telegraph office ? What rent did they pay for a roof or office before ?

Quesnel is nearly two hundred miles from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and is the distributing centre for the whole Cariboo country and the Fraser lakes. I can quite understand that you would not get much of a building in a community of that kind for $2,000. The telegraph station and house is necessary because this is the point of [DOT]onnection with the telegraph line to the Yukon, 200 miles from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Previously, apparently, the telegraph office was in a log building and I presume the operator lived there. I t certainly does not seem to be giving him very luxurious accommodation to erect a frame building at $2,000 to serve the purpose of a living room for him and also of a telegraph office and post office.
What is the population?

The population is not large, but the contributory country is important and it is a distributing centre for that country and also for the Yukon.
Vancouver public building, $150,000.

This vote Is needed for the public building in Vancouver which is now under contract. This is a very fine building but I think no finer or more expensive than is required in a large and growing city like Vancouver. We paid for the site $52,000 and the contract price is $434,500. There was quite a large number of tenders received and the highest for a building of Agassiz granite was $669,000. The lowest, that of Kelly Bros. & Mitchell, of Winnipeg, was $434,500, something like $230,000 less than the highest tender.
(Mr. OWEN. What is the size of the lot?
144 by 175 feet.
The building is 156 feet by 120 feet.
Is the building on a piece of ground entirely separated from
other buildings or is it closely in contact with other buildings ?
It is a corner lot, and at present there is no building close to it.

I hope the government has secured the land so there will be no danger of other buildings being erected close to it. These are the contractors for the Winnipeg post office, I trust they will not be forced to imitate that building which will cost some $600,000 or $700,000 and is one of the most disgraceful jobs ever perpetrated on a free people. On one side of it is the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' office. At one time this had the appearance of a fairly respectable building but when the post office is erected, the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' office is a comparatively small building. The minister will understand my objection to having other buildings close to xjublic buildings, when I say that in Winnipeg in order to accommodate the Wininpeg ' Free Press ' people they actually cut out a corner of the post office after reaching the first story and thereby reduced the floor space of the post office, simply making a present of light and accommodation to a private individual or to a member of this House.
You should not say that
I always believe in saying the truth.
unless you know it.
I think every one admits that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) is the owner of the Winnipeg * Free Press ' office.
I was not aware of that.

That is not the worst feature of it, although it certainly takes away from the appearance of the building: but at the other end there are a couple of jogs for the accommodaton of a hotel stable, which is said to be owned by the second vice-president of the Liberal party In Winnipeg. I was amused and annoyed when looking out of the windows of the post office to see the heaps of manure just outside the window thrown out from the hotel stable close to the post office building. Do they expect the officials to sit Ihrr? and work under such conditions all to oblige the political friends of the government? I once asked the Minister of Public Works how he arrived at an estimate of that building and why it was so unshapely and I was told by the minister that he simply gave the architect carte blanche, allowed him to cut it and carve it as he thought fit. I hope that in the erection <of this building in Vancouver we will have something nicer than that.
I am told this is a splendid building.
I hope it will be. I hope it will not be cut and carved up to accommodate any newspaper office or hotel.
It is too late for that now, the building is well along.

I am glad to know that provided there has been no cutting and carving so far. I do hope and trust there is sufficient lands round the building to prevent any other buildings coming in close contact with it It is a pity that in a great commercial city like Winnipeg we should have such a public building. I undertake to say that you cannot find a Liberal, much less a Conservative, in the city of Winnipeg who will say it is a decent building. The people there are ashamed of it. The government should see that those public buildings on which they spend a large amount of money present as fine an appearance on the exterior as well as in the interior and that they will afford the necessary accommodation. I do not grudge the city of Vancouver a reasonable sum for the erection of a public building but I trust the minister will see that the country gets ample value for the money expended and that the public building is not destroyed for the convenience of any neighbouring property.

My information is that the building at Vancouver is a very handsome structure built of Agazziz granite. Those who have seen the building have nothing but words of praise for it. It is said the contractors are carrying out the work in an efficient manner, and, seeing that the highest tender was over $600,000 and that the lowest tender' accepted was $434,000 it would seem that we are getting full value for our money. I have been told that the Winnipeg building is a very handsome one. It would be much more effective, of course, were it built on a corner, but in the city of Winnipeg the best corner lots costs hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Vernon public building, $5,000.
This vote is for the purchase of a site which will cost $7,500, $5,000 of which has been paid. Vernon is a growing town and this building will accommodate customs and post office.
What is the population?

2,500.	.
Mr. BLAIN How much money will be expended?
The ordinary amount in a town of that size is about $30,000.

Vernon is in the Okanagan valley and beautifully located but I have never understood that land was so extremely valuable there that you would

pay $7,500 for the site of a public bull-ding. It is another Cranbrook ease, and the minister had better put Cranbrook and Vernon together and hand them down to his successor as a piece of ministerial folly.
Vernon is situated in the centre of the fruit growing district where I am told land is worth $200 per acre. We tried to get this site cheaper, but we did not succeed.
What is the size of the lot?
We first purchased two lots 50 by 100, and the architect represented it was not sufficient, and then we bought 25 feet by 100 feet making in all 75 feet by 100 feet.
And land costs $200 an acre?
Farm land.

This amounts to about $10,000 an acre. I think I may say to the minister that cultivated land in that valley costs more than $200 an acre, but that does not justify the minister in paying $1 per square foot. The price is altogether out of keeping with the value of the property.

The members from Ontario who live in prosperous growing towns will be surprised to know that in towns in British Columbia, Manitoba, and the west generally, sites for public buildings cost such an enormous sum of money. Here you purchased 7,500 square feet or one-fifth of an acre and you pay $7,500 for it.
Mr. PUGSLEYL This is a corner lot.
And you buy it at the rate of $10,000 an acre.

It would not be more than one-half of that by the acre, and you do not buy town lots by the acre.
Mr. LALOR It must occur to the representatives from the older provinces that these prices for sites for public buildings in the west are exhorbitant and extravagant. In this town of 2,500 population the government is erecting a $30,000 building. The member for that district whoever he is, must have strong influence with the government.

My hon. friend cannot measure growing towns in the west which have sprung up inside of 15 years with some of the Ontario towns which have possibly not increased by 50 people in 10 years. The towns in the west are growing rapidly.
Mushroom style.

They may be mushroom, but they are there to stay. I can tell my hon. friend that I was in Vernon when you could buy property for $10 Mr. HENDERSON.
per front foot, but I know that you cannot get a good corner lot there to-day for one cent less than $100 per front foot. I suppose that we discount the future, but we have seen all our towns grow from nothing to a considerable size, whereas the people of Ontario have seen their towns the same size for the last twenty-five years.
Nonsense.

I am not speaking of the big cities, but of the country towns. The big cities have grown at the expense of the smaller towns. I am not trying to make any invidious comparisons, but if my hon. friend wants to buy a corner lot in the town of Vernon he will have to pay well for it. A corner lot bought in Vancouver some years ago for $52,000 is worth to-day $300,000.
You have only' one Vancouver in your whole province.
Of course, and there is only one in all Canada.
How much has Kamloops grown in ten years?

I know that there are to-day 2,500 people there and that not very long ago there were but a few. Let my hon. friend try and buy a bit of property in the business centre and he will have to pay well for it. * My hon. friend should not compare the smaller towns of Ontario with those of British Columbia and the west, because the latter are going to become great cities.
How much rent does the Postmaster General pay now for the post office there?
The rent allowance is $250 for the post office and $120 for the customs.
What is the income of that post office ?
It is an out-port of Revelstoke. The postal revenue is $4,794.72, the customs duties, $15,009.84 ; the money orders issued. $31,786.26, and the money orders paid, $18,039.14.

This seems an outrageous expenditure. We are going to spend $40,000 in a little town of 2,500 inhabitants when at present the expense of the post office only amounts to $350 or $375 per annum. Why, you will have to pay that for the caretaker of the new building, and in addition be out of the interest on your money and have a lot of extra expense.
When the minister gives the population as 2,500, is that the present population or the population at the last census ?
The present population.
What was thet population at the last census ? We might then form an idea as to the growth of the town.
I have not got that.
When does the hon. minister propose to hand pic-k Ontario in order to find places in which to put up post offices ?

I have been strongly urged to consider the claims of certain towns in Ontario. Some gentlemen have asked me to consider very favourably the town of Aylmer, also Perth and Dundas and quite a number of other nice towns.
Has the minister made any promises ?
No. I limit myself to performances.
I think yon promised to take it into consideration.
And I intend doing so.

If we consider the amount spent in Ontario as compared with the amount received for postal and customs revenue, and then contrast the expenditure in the other provinces with that in Ontario, you will find a hundred dollars in other provinces to one in Ontario. Ontario is decidedly getting the worst of it. This year that province is served worse in that respect than it has been in any other year. The hon. gentleman had better get busy and do justice to Ontario instead of endeavouring to put himself right with the other provinces. I can well imagine that he believes Ontario is hopelessly gone politically, but I do not think that Ontario should be punished to the extent it is because it shows its sense of the iniquity of this administration.

I think my hon. friend ought not to speak so harshly. He himself urged the claim of a certain town in his constituency, but one might well hesitate to erect a public building there because that would prevent our enjoying my hon. friend's eloquence and criticism. Not long after I became minister certain gentlemen came to me from a town in a constituency represented by a Conservative. They said that years ago the old Conservative government erected a post office building there, but although they put holes in the tower to accommodate a clock, they neglected to put in the clock, and these gentlemen wanted to know if I would not make good that omission of the late government. I cheerfully did so.
Is that all you did for Ontario?
That is what I did for one of the small towns. Wait until you see what we shall do for Ontario.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, but so far as Dufferin is concerned, we never got anything. The only thing the minister has done for Ontario is to put a clock in the tower of the post office at Berlin. Possibly it was one of those clocks which the Toronto ' Globe ' has been giving away at $2.50.

Apparently these post offices are just given to towns according to their political influence. I have been making a request for a post office in a town in my riding, which is in more need of a building than any in the catalogue here tonight.
What town js that ?

Macleod. It is a town of 2,000 people or more, with a greater postal revenue than some of these towns where you are putting up buildings that cost $30,000 or over. The people there who come to receive their mail find an office with a space for the public of only about ten by six. But, as I say, the people are served according to the way they vote.
Victoria immigration building, $30,000.
This building is to be on a corner lot, at the corner of Ontario and Simcoe streets. The building is to be fireproof and two stories high.
What is the frontage of the lot?
The frontage is 98 feet on Ontario street.
What will the whole building cost?
The building, including site, electric wiring, heating, fittings and furniture complete will cost $91,180.97.'
Is there a building in Victoria for immigration purposes?

No. My hon. colleague the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) says that for several years there have been no buildings for immigrant purposes in Victoria.
Mr. BENNETT How has this want been filled? And why do you need this accommodation now? We are told the influx of Japanese is stopped. The Chinese who come in must be wealthy, for they must pay a head tax of $500, and the Hindus are not allowed to come further.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Some years ago, there was an old immigration building, but it was burned down. Some immigrants have been detained in the buildings on what we call the Outer Wharf, and some have been taken into the town and housed in cheap boarding houses under the supervision of the medical superintendent at a great deal of inconvenience and trouble.
What immigration is expected that this expenditure should be necessary V
In a large seaport town like Victoria, there is always considerable immigration. The Department of the Interior has urged the erection of this building.

WThat nationality of immigrants?
* ilr. PUGSLEY. I presume of different nationalities. There would be people coming from the United States, from San Francisco and other coast cities, and many of them would come in by Victoria and Vancouver.
Mr. ARMSTRONG What representations have been made to the minister in favour of this building? Though he is going to spend $90,000 on it, he seems to have little information as to the need for it?

I presume the explanation was given last session, when the construction of this building was decided upon. Of the amount now asked, $20,000 is a revote. In the memorandum before me no information is given as to the representations made, and I have no personal knowledge of it, as the matter was decided by parliament before I became minister.
Surely, the deputy minister will be able to advise the hon. gentleman (Mr Pugsley) as to what representations were made to show the necessity for this building?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The request came from the Department of the Interior.
ill1. ARMSTRONG. What is the nature of the request?	-
The request would be for the erection of the building and urging the necessity for it.

For what reason ?
. Mr. PUGSLEY. It would state the requirements and so on.
It is quite evident the minister is merely making that up and has no definite information. We ought to be informed what need exists for the construction of this building.

Tbe minister (Mr. Pugsley) speaks of immigrants coming from the United States. He will hardly contend that such immigrants come in by way of Victoria. If we are going to have immigration of Japanese, this building may be necessary. But even the Japanese, I think, will come in by way of Vancouver, and not Victoria. I do not see what purpose this building can serve.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: Can the minister inform us what number of immigrants have come in by Victoria during the last five years? If we had this or any other definite information, we could judge of the need of this building. I do not object to spending money where it is usefully spent, but I do think that, in view of the present agitation against oriental immigration, there cannot be any possible use of a building to cost $90,000. The hon. member for Muslcoka (Mr. Wright) says this can hardly be intended, as the minister has suggested, to accommodate immigrants from the United States. We know that farmers coming from the middle states into Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan are not going to come in by way of Victoria. But let us have some data to go upon.

I presume that the matter was discussed when this vote was before the committee last session-either that, or hon. gentlemen opposite saw no objection to the vote. Pursuant to that vote of parliament, steps were taken to enter into a contract, and a contract has been entered into. Therefore, it is too late now to refuse to go on.

To whom has the contract been let?
ilr. PUGSLEY. To Luney Brothers, of Victoria. In order that hon. members may be afforded every opportunity to criticise items, I will obtain from the Minister of the Interior the figures as to the immigration for five years. An opportunity will be given to discuss the matter on another item. But I think it is too late to discuss the question of putting up the building seeing that the contract has been entered into.

That seems a pretty flimsy excuse for spending $90,000 on a new building-no explanation what it is to be used for or what is the need for it. There is no objection on this side, so far as I can learn, to the expenditure of this money if we are told that it is spent for a useful purpose. The minister is unable to give us any information, although he has his deputies with him.
What information does the hon. gentleman want ?
We have been asking the minister to tell where the representations came from. If the minister is spending $90,000, he ought to have some knowledge of the requirements.

I have explained to the committee that previous to the last session of parliament there was a request from the Minister of the Interior, who has charge of the Department of Immigration, that this building was required in Victoria for the accommodation of immigrants. In pursu-
1QS77

auce of that request at the last session of parliament a vote of $20,000 was asked for. That vote was passed by parliament, and in consequence the necessary steps were taken for the purpose of entering into a contract. The contract has been entered into, and I now ask for a sum of money to pay the contractors on account. This building is being erected in accordance with the requirements of the Department of the Interior.
When was the contract entered into ?
On the 23rd of January, 1908.
Where will the building be situated?
On the southwest corner of Ontario and Simcoe streets.

It is true that the same number and class jtf immigrants do not arrive in British Columbia as arrive from Europe on the Atlantic coast. But the House must remember that the city of Victoria is the first port of call for all steamers arriving in British Columbia. We have lines of steamers running to Japan and China, and several Japanese lines also making regular trips. We have the blue funnel lines running from British Columbia via the Indian ocean to Liverpool, carrying freight and passengers ; we have a line of steamers running to Australia, a line to New Zealand, a San Francisco boat every five days, and we have a line of steamers running to Mexico. All these steamers call at the city of Victoria, and while the number of passengers cannot compare with the number arriving at the Atlantic ports, nevertheless many do come into Victoria and pass on to other places. All steamers call first at quarantine seven miles away, and then come on to Victoria where most of the passengers disembark. While many of the passengers in years past have been Orientals of various classes, there are nevertheless many whites coming in from Australia, some from San Francisco, and some from New Zealand. During the Klondike excitement a great many came from Australia. Although the necessity for an immigration building is not so great on the Pacific ocean as it is on the Atlantic, nevertheless there is a great necessity for one. Even the limited number of Japanese and Chinese who are coming into the country, may be required to be detained at the immigration building for some days or weeks. This is probably the only building in British Columbia designed for" this purpose. We have in Vancouver a building that is rented from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and which is used to a considerable extent for this purpose. This building is conveniently situated, quite 345
near the wharf. The site is a large block of land, on which an old immigration building. a wooden structure, was burnt down some years ago. That land will be utilized for this purpose, along with several additional lots. The building will stand isolated. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that there is great necessity for it. The request for the building came altogether from the Interior Department. I was notified by the Interior Department of their intention to erect this building a year or so ago. But I had nothing to do with it myself, nor do I know of any one else who had anything to do with it ; the erection of the building is a purely departmental affair.
Do I understand that no petitions came from Victoria asking for this building ? The hou. gentleman said just now that the department were responsible for erecting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is perfectly absurd that petitions should come from any city, in any part of Canada, for the erection of an immigration building. No city anywhere is particularly desirous of seeing an immigration building erected in its midst. In the city of Victoria, were it not for the fact that this government own probably one-half of the plot of ground proposed to be used for this purpose, I do not think this building would be erected on the proposed site. Victoria prides herself on being one of the most beautiful cities in Canada. This particular site is near the Dallas hotel where a great many tourists reside, and some citizens do not want that immigration building there, and it would not lie there were not for the fact that the government own the land. The ' building will be a plain brick structure, but it will not disfigure the beauty of the locality. Since the old wooden building was burnt down some years ago, the government have been doing the best they could in caring for the immigrants.
What percentage of the immigrants that landed at Victoria were Japanese ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Last year a very large percentage; 0,000 or 7,000 came into British Columbia last year.

I find by the returns that there were only 2,293 immigrants landed at Victoria. It does seem to me that $90,000 is an extravagant expenditure for the number of immigrants that are likely to enter British Columbia from the west. It is not to be expected that there will be much European immigration into British Columbia, and to expend $90,000 for Japanese immigration that only amounted to sixteen hundred and sixty-six last year seems to me extravagant.

Land seems to be so valuable in these western cities that I should have thought the government would have sold this site, which I understand is close to one of the leading hotels and bought at the outskirts of the city where they could have secured a site much more cheaply.
My hon. friend will see the necessity of having the immigration building close to the incoming steamers.
Will the minister tell us how this building is to be fitted up ? At a cost of .$90,000 it must be a palace.

It has a frontage of 98 feet on Ontario street and it is to be two stories with a basement. It is to have varandahs 10 feet in width on both stories extending along both sides. The walls are to be of brick on concrete foundations, the basement above ground being faced with stone and the verandahs being constructed of iron and concrete. In the basement there is to be a boiler room, fuel room, storage, &c., The building is pretty nearly fire proof.

Which minister ?

If my hon. friend will pardon me we will come to that later.

My tastes are not luxurious.
In the nine months, ended March 31, 1906, Japanese immigrants arrived to the number of 720 while in the nine months, ended March 31, 1907, they number 1,666, an increase of

916 with a total immigration of 2,293.' I do not know why the government are erecting a building there. You do not want Japanese immigration and yet you are erecting a building at a cost of over $90,000 to accommodate 627 immigrants annually according to these figures. I think that as the Minister of the Interior is not here he ought to be sent for or the item ought to stand until we get the information because it is simply outrageous to think that for the accommodation of 627 immigrants a year we are going to spend $90,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The steamers arriving from the Orient bring passengers from Japan with passports for the United States. These steamers disembark .their passengers at Victoria in many cases. The ' Empress ' steamers certainly disembark their passengers at A'ietoria. The passengers have to wait there to take the local steamer to Seattle or Tacoma.
Have we to provide accommodation for all transients ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Unfortunately, that is the state of affairs. These steamers may disembark 400 or 500 people with passports for the United States. They have no right to come into Canada. They may be refused the right to land in the United States for various reasons or they may escape into Victoria, but it is the duty of our officers to see that passengers with passports for the United States shall go to the United States. The ocean steamers land at the outer wharf and this new building is contiguous to it. These passengers are corralled there for a time and then sent over to the United States. Sometimes they may have to remain if they are suffering from simple diseases and they must be put in the immigration building to be taken care of. The responsibility rests upon our immigration officials to see that these passengers go to their destination and it is necessary they should be housed probably for a night or two. I do not know the number of immigrants who have come into British Columbia during the last year or two but there is no question that a building is necessary at Victoria.
How many immigration officials have we at Victoria ?
ATery few. There is the medical officer and I think he has two assistants, or, he may have but one.

If Japanese are coming across on our boats, or on any other boats, destined to the Uinted States ports, they ought not to be allowed to land until

they arrive at the United States ports. If they are allowed to land it looks like very lax management and it is something which onght to be corrected.

Passengers coming by the Empresses, for instance, destined for ports in the United States, such as San Francisco, Seattle or Tacoma must disembark at Victoria or Vancouver to take the coast steamers for their destinations in the United States. It is certainly a very proper and humane thing to have a place where these people can be kept temporarily until the coast steamer leaves so that they may be sent, off to their destination.

This is a very serious state of affairs and much more light should be shed upon this vote before it is allowed to pass. It is extraordinary that we should have to provide for the Japanese and Chinese who pass through our country on their way to the United States. Vancouver and the other British Columbia cities are almost in rebellion against the immigration of Japanese and Chinese, and if these immigrants are allowed to land there is danger of them escaping to the interior of the country in hundreds.

Strathroy $13,000, and Walkerton $8,700. These are partly constructed. I do not know how much of this $50,000 will be needed to complete them. What about carrying out your arrangement at Gananoque ?

I had forgotten about it but I will look into it again.

It is my wish that wherever there is an isolated company it should have a home of its own with accommodation for arms and accoutrements and a sort of lecture room where the members of the company could meet in the evening and hear lectures.

Certainly. That is my ideal, but I regret I have not been able to carry it out. I do not quarrel with the Department of Public Works, but

the minister sometimes thinks we are too extravagant. 1 may say that the engineers in my department have made plans which would give us buildings ranging from $2,500 for a single company armoury up to $10,000 for a regimental headquarters armoury. that the building is a very handsome one, that it is a credit to the city of London. It would be a shame to have anything else in a city like London, one of the finest on the continent.

I do not object to London getting a fair armoury, but I wanted other places to be recognized as well. While London is an important city, it has nearly always had a disorganized regiment. Occasionally it bursts up and is reorganized.
